patient_information: A 7-year-old girl who lives in Lima, Peru. She is described as otherwise healthy.
chief_complaint: A chronic skin lesion on the nose for four months.
history_of_present_illness: The lesion appeared four months ago as a small nodule and slowly evolved into an ulcer. It is reported to be slightly itchy but not painful. There is no history of trauma to the area.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The patient lives in Lima, the capital of Peru. Six months prior to presentation, she travelled to a valley on the western slopes of the Andes, an area known to be endemic for leishmaniasis. She resides in a poor neighborhood with a high incidence of tuberculosis.
vitals: She was afebrile during the clinical examination.
physical_exam: Examination revealed a localized ulcer on the nose, approximately 2 cm in diameter, with indurated borders and plaque-like infiltration of the surrounding skin. After removal of a scab, the ulcer had a cobblestone-patterned bottom and raised edges. There were no palpable lymph nodes, and the rest of the physical examination was normal.
labs_and_diagnostics: Microscopic examination of a smear obtained by scraping the lesion was negative. The leishmanin skin test was positive. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was also positive, and the infecting species was identified as Leishmania (Viannia) peruviana.
differential_diagnosis: The differential diagnoses included infectious causes of facial lesions such as cutaneous leishmaniasis, sporotrichosis, cutaneous tuberculosis, and Balamuthia mandrillaris infection. Cutaneous leishmaniasis was considered most likely due to the patient's travel to an endemic area and the characteristic presentation of a painless ulcer with raised borders. Cutaneous tuberculosis was a consideration due to her living in a high-incidence area, while sporotrichosis was less likely as she had not visited a hyperendemic region for it. Other diagnoses like anthrax and tularemia were deemed inconsistent with the clinical course and location.
management_and_clinical_course: The patient was treated with intravenous sodium stibogluconate (SSG) at a dose of 20 mg/kg/day for 20 days. Concurrently, she received topical imiquimod therapy every other day for 20 days. The response to treatment was good, and at a three-month follow-up visit, she showed no signs of relapse.
final_diagnosis: The final diagnosis is cutaneous leishmaniasis caused by the protozoan parasite Leishmania (Viannia) peruviana. The diagnosis was established based on the characteristic clinical presentation of a chronic, painless ulcer on the nose, a relevant travel history to an endemic region in Peru, a positive leishmanin skin test, and definitive confirmation by a positive polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test which identified the causative species, despite a negative microscopic smear.
